title: When to enroll in Medicare
summary: Guide to when and how to enroll in Medicare, covering automatic enrollment, all enrollment periods, disability enrollment, working past 65, spouse coverage, Social Security, and HSAs.

atoms.title: Automatic Medicare enrollment at 65
atoms.question: Will I be enrolled in Medicare automatically at 65?
atoms.text: If you start receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits before you turn 65, you should be enrolled in Medicare automatically. If you are not enrolled automatically, you will need to sign up by yourself: online at www.ssa.gov, in person at your local Social Security office, or by phone at 1-800-772-1213 / TTY 1-800-325-0778. You may not be notified when you become eligible, so find your Initial Enrollment Period dates and put them in your calendar.

atoms.title: Initial Enrollment Period at age 65
atoms.question: When does my Initial Enrollment Period start and end when I turn 65?
atoms.text: If you first become eligible for Medicare because you are turning 65, your Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) begins three months before the month of your 65th birthday and ends three months afterward. During your IEP, you can enroll in Original Medicare (Part A and/or Part B), a Medicare Advantage plan or a Part D prescription drug plan without penalty. Medicare Advantage plans may not be available in all states or territories.

atoms.title: General Enrollment Period (GEP)
atoms.question: What is the Medicare General Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: The General Enrollment Period (GEP) lets you enroll in Original Medicare Part B if you missed your Initial Enrollment Period and do not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. If you don't qualify for premium-free Part A and missed your IEP, you can also buy Part A during this time. The GEP runs from January 1 to March 31, and when you enroll during it, your coverage starts the first day of the month after you sign up.

atoms.title: Special Enrollment Period triggers
atoms.question: What is a Medicare Special Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: A Special Enrollment Period (SEP) gives you a chance to change plans after certain life events, such as moving out of your plan's service area, your plan changing its contract with Medicare, losing your current health insurance including from your employer, having an opportunity to get other coverage from your employer or union, or being affected by a disaster or emergency.

atoms.title: Annual Enrollment Period (AEP)
atoms.question: When is the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: The Annual Enrollment Period (AEP) is the time each year when you can sign up for a Medicare Advantage plan, switch Medicare Advantage plans, or join or leave a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan. It begins October 15 and ends December 7. Changes made during AEP take effect the following January 1.

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period
atoms.question: What is the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: The Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period (OEP) is when you can switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another, with or without drug coverage, or leave a Medicare Advantage plan and return to Original Medicare and enroll in a Part D prescription drug plan if you choose. It begins January 1 and ends March 31 every year.

atoms.title: Medicare enrollment with a disability
atoms.question: When can I enroll in Medicare if I have a disability or medical condition?
atoms.text: With a qualifying disability, you should become eligible for Medicare after you have received SSDI benefits for 24 months. Your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period will include your 25th month of disability, the 3 months before and the 3 months after. You may also qualify for Medicare due to Lou Gehrig's disease (ALS) or end-stage renal disease (ESRD), and your IEP may depend on your diagnosis.

atoms.title: Delaying Medicare while working past 65
atoms.question: Do I need Medicare if I work past age 65?
atoms.text: If you expect to continue working past age 65, you may want to delay enrolling in Medicare. If you have health coverage from your employer or are covered under a spouse's employer plan, you may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period and be able to delay enrolling without penalty. In some situations, such as working for an employer with fewer than 20 employees, you may still be required to take full Medicare benefits at age 65 even if you plan to keep working.

atoms.title: Enrolling later after delaying Medicare
atoms.question: If I delay Medicare now, how do I enroll later?
atoms.text: If you are eligible for Medicare, delay enrollment past age 65 and have health insurance through your employer, you can enroll later in a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) when you retire or lose coverage. During this 8-month period you can enroll in Original Medicare (Part A and/or Part B). You can also enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan or a Part D plan, but you only get the first 2 months of your SEP to do so without penalty.

atoms.title: Medicare and a spouse's insurance
atoms.question: Do I need Medicare if I am covered by my spouse's insurance?
atoms.text: If you have insurance through a spouse's employer, you may be able to delay enrollment in Medicare past age 65. This depends on the employer's rules for covered dependents of Medicare age. Talk with the employer's benefits administrator to learn what you can do about Medicare enrollment.

atoms.title: Medicare vs Social Security eligibility
atoms.question: Is Medicare eligibility the same as Social Security eligibility?
atoms.text: No. Medicare eligibility and benefits are separate from Social Security eligibility and benefits. You can enroll in Medicare at age 65 or with a qualifying disability or medical condition, while your Social Security eligibility depends on what year you were born, when you retire and other factors.

atoms.title: How Medicare enrollment affects your HSA
atoms.question: How will Medicare enrollment affect my Health Savings Account?
atoms.text: Once you enroll in Medicare Part A or Part B, you can no longer make pre-tax contributions to your HSA. If you receive Social Security benefits, Part A is generally automatic and coverage is retroactive for up to 6 months, so you should plan to stop contributing to your HSA about 6 months before enrolling. You can keep contributing if you are eligible for Medicare but have not enrolled, and after enrolling you can still withdraw HSA funds tax-free for some Medicare expenses and qualified medical expenses.
